title: GLM Transit: The Maglev Web
body:
# GLM Transit: The Maglev Web

## The Network

The Great Lakes Metropolitan maglev network is the largest integrated magnetic levitation transit system in the Western Hemisphere. It connects six US states, two Canadian provinces, and approximately 40 million people through 4,800 kilometers of elevated and sublacustrine guideway. It moves 6.2 million passengers daily. It is the circulatory system of the GLM, and like all circulatory systems, where the blood flows determines what lives and what dies.

Construction began in 2151 under the first GLM Compact infrastructure mandate. Kessler-Dyne won the primary construction contract — 60% of the network by kilometer — with Meridian 88 building the Chicago corridor and NovaChem handling the Canadian segments through their Ontario subsidiary. The first operational segment, Milwaukee to Chicago, opened in 2158. Full network completion, including the sublacustrine lake crossings and the Canadian connections, was declared in 2174, though expansion has continued steadily since.

The technology is superconducting electromagnetic suspension — the guideway contains superconducting coils cooled by liquid nitrogen, generating the magnetic field that levitates and propels the train cars. There are no wheels, no friction, no contact between vehicle and track. The cars float on a magnetic cushion 15 centimeters above the guideway surface and accelerate via linear motor — sequential electromagnetic pulses along the guideway that push the vehicle forward like a series of magnetic kicks.

Operating speed: 500-600 km/h for express routes. 200-300 km/h for local service. A passenger boarding the maglev in Milwaukee reaches Chicago in 11 minutes. Detroit in 45 minutes. Cleveland in 68 minutes. Toronto in 82 minutes. The GLM, which by highway distances spans over 1,500 kilometers, is compressed by the maglev into a region where no two points are more than 90 minutes apart.

## The Routes

The network is organized into three tiers of service:

**Express Corridor (the Spine).** The primary east-west route running from Milwaukee through Chicago, Gary, South Bend, Toledo, Cleveland, and terminating at Buffalo. A single unbroken guideway, 900 kilometers, with six stops. Express service runs every 8 minutes during peak hours, every 15 minutes off-peak. The Spine carries 2.1 million passengers daily and is the single most heavily used transit route in North America. It is also the route most tightly controlled by corponation interests — Meridian 88 operates the Chicago segment, Kessler-Dyne operates Milwaukee to Gary and Toledo to Cleveland, and NovaChem operates the Buffalo terminal through a joint venture.

**Regional Connectors (the Ribs).** North-south routes branching from the Spine to serve the broader GLM territory. The Milwaukee-Green Bay Connector. The Chicago-Springfield Connector (the longest Rib at 340 kilometers). The Detroit-Saginaw Connector. The Cleveland-Columbus Connector. The cross-lake routes: Milwaukee-Muskegon (sublacustrine), Chicago-Holland (sublacustrine), and the controversial Detroit-Windsor Connector that crosses the international border. There are fourteen Ribs in total, carrying 3.4 million passengers daily at express and local speeds.

**Local Networks (the Capillaries).** Within each major metropolitan area, local maglev networks connect neighborhoods, districts, and arcology complexes. These are lower-speed systems (120-200 km/h) with frequent stops. The Chicago Capillary network alone has 240 stations. Milwaukee's has 86. Detroit's has 112. The Capillaries are where the tier system bites hardest.

## Tier-Segregated Service

The maglev network is technically available to all GLM residents with valid neural ID. In practice, access is stratified by tier in ways that are architecturally enforced, economically coercive, and socially absolute.

**Tier 5 (Executive).** Private cars. A Tier 5 passenger never shares a maglev car with anyone outside their security detail. The cars are custom-fitted — NovaChem's executive fleet features individual cabins with full communications suites, refreshment service, and Faraday shielding that blocks neural scanning. The cars attach to express trains at designated VIP platforms that are physically separated from public boarding areas. A Tier 5 passenger boarding in Chicago sees no one below Tier 4 between their vehicle and their destination. Cost: included in corporate compensation packages. No Tier 5 individual pays for transit out of personal funds.

**Tier 4 (Professional).** Reserved sections in express cars. Climate-controlled, low-density seating, priority boarding. The Tier 4 sections are separated from Tier 3 by physical barriers — transparent but locked partitions that open only for neural IDs reading Tier 4 or above. A Tier 4 passenger can see the Tier 3 section through the glass. The view is instructive. Cost: Φ2,400 annually for unlimited Spine and Rib access.

**Tier 3 (Standard).** General boarding on all express and local services. Tier 3 passengers constitute the majority of ridership — approximately 65% of all trips. The cars are functional but not comfortable: standing room during peak hours, limited climate control, basic seating that accommodates but does not pamper. A Tier 3 worker commuting from a Milwaukee residential arcology to a Chicago industrial district spends 45-60 minutes each way in conditions comparable to 2125 subway service, compressed into a vehicle traveling at 500 km/h. Cost: Φ800 annually, automatically deducted from employment wages. Not optional — transit access is a condition of formal employment.

**Tier 2 (Marginal).** Restricted to local networks only. No Spine access. No Rib access except during designated off-peak windows (0100-0500). A Tier 2 resident of Gary cannot commute to Chicago by maglev during working hours. This single restriction functionally limits Tier 2 employment options to their immediate local area, which in most cases offers only manual labor, hazard-class industrial work, or the informal economy. Tier 2 passengers board from separate platforms — often underground or in service corridors — and ride in utility cars originally designed for maintenance crew transport. Cost: Φ200 annually. The affordability is irrelevant — the access restrictions make the pass nearly worthless for economic mobility.

**Tier 1 (Excluded).** No maglev access. Tier 1 residents — the unregistered, the tier-stripped, the populations living in Dead Zones and peripheral settlements — cannot board any maglev service. Their neural ID (if they have one) is flagged at every boarding gate. Attempting to board triggers security response. The maglev network connects 40 million people. Approximately 4 million residents of the GLM territory are Tier 1. They walk, they ride unlicensed vehicles, they use the tunnel network if they can access it, or they don't travel. The maglev web is not for them. It was never designed to be.

## The Sublacustrine Crossings

The three cross-lake maglev routes are engineering achievements and security nightmares. The Milwaukee-Muskegon crossing runs 130 kilometers through a pressurized tunnel 60 meters below the Lake Michigan surface. Transit time: 14 minutes. The tunnel is a single point of failure — if the guideway is disrupted, if the tunnel integrity is compromised, if the power supply is interrupted, 2,000-4,000 passengers are trapped in a tube under a lake with limited emergency egress.

Security is accordingly intense. Every sublacustrine crossing has redundant power (three independent feeds), redundant pressurization (four atmospheric processing units per kilometer), and emergency escape pods positioned every 500 meters — pressurized capsules that can surface autonomously if the tunnel floods. The escape pods are tested monthly. They have never been used in an actual emergency. No one wants to find out whether they work.

The crossings are also chokepoints for smuggling interdiction. Every passenger and cargo container passing through a sublacustrine tunnel is scanned — neural ID verification, cargo manifest cross-reference, and passive chemical sampling for prohibited materials. The tunnels are the one place in the GLM where movement is absolutely controlled, absolutely monitored, and absolutely documented. Which is why the Bore Rats never use them.

## Maintenance and Vulnerability

The maglev network requires continuous maintenance that is invisible to passengers and critical to survival. The superconducting coils must be kept below 77 Kelvin (-196°C) — any interruption in the liquid nitrogen cooling system causes the coils to lose superconductivity, the magnetic field collapses, and the levitating car drops 15 centimeters onto the guideway at whatever speed it's traveling. At 500 km/h, the result is catastrophic.

There have been three coil failures in the network's operational history. The worst, in 2189 on the Spine near Toledo, killed 342 passengers when an express car de-levitated at 540 km/h and disintegrated against the guideway walls. The cause was a nitrogen supply line failure caused by corrosion — maintenance had been deferred for six months due to a contract dispute between Kessler-Dyne and the GLM Compact Commission over cost allocation.

Three hundred forty-two people died because of a contract dispute. The maglev still runs. The contract disputes continue. The nitrogen lines corrode at the same rate they always have.
